Rhinitis

the step-up ladder · nasal steroid after antihistamines fail · start 2 weeks before pollen · immunotherapy is the baitWhich step has the patient already failed, and how far off is the pollen season?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Moderate to severe seasonal rhinitis that has failed antihistamines an intranasal corticosteroid, the most effective drug class
  • Seen in late winter start it about 2 weeks before pollen season; it needs lead time
  • Immunotherapy only after drug therapy fails; a decongestant spray past 3 days rebound congestion
What it is

Allergic rhinitis: a type I hypersensitivity of the nasal mucosa, for example to pollen

Driver

Allergen IgE (immunoglobulin E)-mediated reaction eosinophil-rich mucosal inflammation

Triggers

Pollen, dust, animal dander

Atopy: asthma and eczema travel with it

Chain

Exposure sneezing, itch, clear rhinorrhea, congestion pale, boggy turbinates

Repeated bouts nasal polyps

Insights

Itchy, watery eyes point to allergic rhinitis; vasomotor rhinitis spares the eyes

A first-generation antihistamine in the stem is usually there to be replaced, not continued

3Differential
Look-alikes, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Allergic rhinitisSneezing, itch, clear rhinorrhea; pale, boggy mucosaWith exposure, eg pollen season; eye symptoms
Vasomotor rhinitis (nonallergic rhinitis)Clear rhinorrhea set off by temperature change; no itch or sneezingNo eye symptoms; no response to oral antihistamines
Rhinitis medicamentosaWorse congestion on a decongestant spraySpray used past 3 days; rebound vasodilation
Viral rhinitis (common cold)Sneezing, congestion, runny noseA cold; rhinovirus the usual cause
Nasal foreign bodyA young child with nasal dischargeOne side, foul-smelling, purulent or bloody
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Seen in late winter, before pollen seasonProphylaxisStart the nasal steroid about 2 weeks before the season
Rhinitis with asthma, wants one oral drugMontelukastCounsel on neuropsychiatric effects

Pause point. The bait: immunotherapy, the only option that changes the disease, offered to a patient who has never tried a nasal steroid. Desensitization waits until drug therapy fails.

7Treatment
1

Avoidwhen practical

Allergen avoidance

Practical for dust mites or pets; not for pollen, where limiting time outdoors fails.

2

1st linemoderate to severe, or antihistamines failing

An intranasal corticosteroid

It suppresses the mucosal inflammation and needs lead time: start about 2 weeks before pollen season.

3

Addsymptoms persist

A second-generation antihistamine, oral or intranasal

First-generation agents sedate and are anticholinergic: replace them.

4

Lastdrug therapy fails

Allergen immunotherapy (desensitization)

Rising allergen doses shift the response from IgE to IgG (immunoglobulin G); the only disease-modifying option.

First treatment by situation
SituationChooseWatch for
Vasomotor rhinitisAn intranasal antihistamine (azelastine) or intranasal steroidOral antihistamines do not work
Rhinitis medicamentosaStop the decongestant sprayLimit sprays such as oxymetazoline to 3 days
Rhinitis with asthma, one oral drug wantedWatch forLess effective than a nasal steroid, and it carries a boxed warning from the Food and Drug Administration for neuropsychiatric effects; counsel if it is chosen.Neuropsychiatric effects
Nasal foreign body in a childPositive pressure: blow out with the other nostril held shutFoul, one-sided discharge
Any rhinitisNot oral prednisoneSystemic steroids for a benign chronic condition
Practice
  1. 28 yo F with moderate seasonal rhinitis failing OTC antihistamines → Intranasal corticosteroid
  2. 28 yo F seeking durable control after several drug classes have failed → Allergen immunotherapy
  3. 28 yo F advised to minimize outdoor activity for her pollen allergy → Impractical for pollen, unlike dust-mite control
  4. 28 yo F with rhinitis and asthma who wants a single oral agent → Montelukast – with neuropsychiatric counseling
  5. 28 yo F using oxymetazoline for 10 days with worsening congestion → Rhinitis medicamentosa → stop the spray
  6. 28 yo F with clear rhinorrhea, no itch or sneezing, triggered by temperature change → Vasomotor rhinitis
